questions.stem: Under the treaty reporting system, a state that is party to a human rights treaty must:
options: let UN officials review every bill before it is introduced into parliament
submit all its court decisions on human rights to the International Court of Justice
send regular reports to the treaty's committee on how it is meeting its obligations
ask the Security Council for approval before passing any law affecting rights
questions.explanation: Each core treaty has a committee of independent experts, and states parties report to it periodically on the measures they have taken. The committee then issues concluding observations with its concerns and recommendations. There is no UN approval of bills.

questions.stem: After examining Australia's report, the Committee on the Rights of the Child issues concluding observations recommending changes to youth justice laws. What is the legal status of these recommendations?
options: They automatically amend any Australian law found to be inconsistent
They are binding only if the Security Council later adopts them
They are not binding, but they apply diplomatic and public pressure
They are binding orders that Australian courts must enforce immediately
questions.explanation: Concluding observations are authoritative recommendations rather than binding orders. Their force comes from public scrutiny, media attention and diplomatic pressure, and from their use by advocates and parliaments. They do not change domestic law by themselves.

questions.stem: The UN treaty body that monitors states' compliance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights is the:
options: Human Rights Council
Security Council
International Court of Justice
Human Rights Committee
questions.explanation: The Human Rights Committee is a body of 18 independent experts set up under the ICCPR to examine state reports and individual complaints. The Human Rights Council is a separate body of UN member states that runs the Universal Periodic Review and appoints Special Rapporteurs.

questions.stem: The Australian Human Rights Commission and several non-government organisations send the treaty committee their own reports on Australia's human rights record. These are often called:
options: concluding observations, which the state must adopt within twelve months
shadow reports, giving committees an independent view of the record
advisory opinions, which bind the committee when it writes its observations
reservations, which limit the obligations Australia must report on
questions.explanation: National human rights institutions and NGOs act as ancillary bodies by submitting shadow or parallel reports, which help committees test the government's account. Advisory opinions come from the ICJ, and concluding observations are written by the committee itself.

questions.stem: The Universal Periodic Review is best described as:
options: a trial of state leaders accused of serious human rights abuses, run by the ICC
a review of a state's treaty reservations, run by the UN Secretary-General
a peer review of every UN member state's record, run by the Human Rights Council
a review of a state's compliance with one treaty, run by that treaty's committee of experts
questions.explanation: Under the Universal Periodic Review, every UN member state, including Australia, has its human rights record examined by other states in the Human Rights Council and receives recommendations, which it may accept or note. It applies to all states regardless of which treaties they have ratified.

questions.stem: A UN Special Rapporteur on a human rights theme visits Australia at the government's invitation, meets officials and community groups, and reports to the Human Rights Council. Which statement about Special Rapporteurs is correct?
options: They are UN judges who can order a state to change its laws after a visit
They are Australian public servants who represent Australia at the UN
They are diplomats appointed by the Security Council to negotiate treaties
They are independent experts who report but cannot enforce findings
questions.explanation: Special Rapporteurs are independent experts appointed under the Human Rights Council's special procedures, with a thematic or country mandate. They visit countries, receive communications and report publicly, but their findings are recommendations rather than binding orders.

questions.stem: Article 41 of the ICCPR allows one state to complain that another state is not meeting its obligations. Why has this inter-State complaint process rarely been used?
options: Both states must accept it, and states avoid accusing each other
Only the five permanent members of the Security Council are allowed to use it
Complaints must first be approved by a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly
It applies only to disputes about borders, not to disputes about human rights
questions.explanation: The procedure works only between states that have both declared they accept it, and governments are usually reluctant to damage relations by formally accusing another state. As a result, monitoring relies mostly on reporting, the Universal Periodic Review and individual complaints.

questions.stem: An individual can complain to the Human Rights Committee that Australia has breached their ICCPR rights because Australia has:
options: ratified the Rome Statute and the person has been charged with a serious crime
accepted the jurisdiction of the ICJ for all disputes involving its own citizens
passed a national bill of rights that allows appeals to the United Nations
acceded to the First Optional Protocol and the person has exhausted domestic remedies
questions.explanation: The First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR, which took effect for Australia in December 1991, lets individuals complain to the Human Rights Committee. The person must first exhaust available domestic remedies. Only states can be parties to ICJ cases.

questions.stem: In Toonen v Australia (1994), the Human Rights Committee found that Tasmanian laws criminalising sex between consenting adult men breached the right to privacy in the ICCPR. What happened next?
options: Tasmania's laws were immediately invalid, because the Committee's views bind Australian courts
The ICJ ordered Australia to pay compensation to Mr Toonen within twelve months
Australia withdrew from the First Optional Protocol to avoid further complaints
The Commonwealth passed a law protecting sexual privacy, and Tasmania later repealed its laws
questions.explanation: The Committee's views were not binding, but the Commonwealth responded with legislation protecting private sexual conduct between adults, and Tasmania repealed its laws in 1997 after further litigation. The case shows international monitoring influencing domestic law through political pressure.

questions.stem: The Human Rights Committee finds that Australia breached a person's rights by keeping him in immigration detention, and asks Australia to compensate him. Australia does not do so. What does this best show about the complaints system?
options: It depends on a state's willingness to comply, as views cannot be enforced
It is binding on Australia, so the person can enforce the views in the Federal Court
It allows the Security Council to impose sanctions whenever a state ignores views
It applies only to states that have no human rights protections of their own
questions.explanation: The Committee's views are authoritative interpretations of the ICCPR, but there is no mechanism to enforce them. Compliance depends on political will, public pressure and a state's concern for its international reputation.

questions.stem: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is located in The Hague and is made up of:
options: 18 experts elected by states parties to the ICCPR
12 judges, one from each permanent member and region
15 judges elected for nine-year terms
9 judges appointed for life by the Secretary-General
questions.explanation: The ICJ, the principal judicial organ of the UN, has 15 judges elected by the General Assembly and Security Council for nine-year terms. The 18 experts belong to the Human Rights Committee.

questions.stem: Which of the following could be a party to a contentious case before the International Court of Justice?
options: Australia, in a dispute with another state that accepts the court's jurisdiction
An Australian citizen, in a complaint that her right to privacy was breached
A former military commander, charged with war crimes committed overseas
A multinational company, in a contract dispute with a foreign government
questions.explanation: Only states can be parties to contentious cases at the ICJ, and the court's jurisdiction depends on their consent. Individuals accused of international crimes are tried by the ICC or national courts, and individual human rights complaints go to treaty bodies.

questions.stem: In Whaling in the Antarctic (Australia v Japan) (2014), the ICJ found that Japan's whaling program was not for purposes of scientific research and ordered Japan to revoke its permits. This case shows that the ICJ:
options: can resolve disputes between states about their obligations under a treaty
can convict the individuals responsible for breaching environmental treaties
can hear cases only when the Security Council refers them to the court
can decide disputes only between states in the same region of the world
questions.explanation: Australia brought the case under the International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling, and both states had accepted the court's jurisdiction. The ICJ decides disputes between states; it does not convict individuals, and it does not need a Security Council referral.

questions.stem: After the whaling judgment, Japan stopped its Antarctic program but later withdrew from the International Whaling Commission and resumed commercial whaling in its own waters. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Australia could then bring a criminal case against Japan's leaders in the ICJ
A state can comply yet use its sovereignty to change its obligations
The ICJ's judgments have no legal force, so Japan never had to comply with it
The Security Council must enforce every ICJ judgment by sending peacekeepers
questions.explanation: ICJ judgments are binding on the parties, and Japan complied by revoking the permits. However, a sovereign state can withdraw from a treaty organisation and so change its future obligations, which shows the limits of international law. The ICJ never hears criminal cases.

questions.stem: In 2025 the ICJ gave an advisory opinion, requested by the General Assembly, on the obligations of states in respect of climate change. Which statement about ICJ advisory opinions is correct?
options: They are binding orders that require named states to pay damages
They can be requested by any individual who is affected by the issue
They replace the need for states to ratify the relevant treaties
They clarify international law for UN bodies but are not binding on states
questions.explanation: Advisory opinions are given at the request of authorised UN organs and agencies, such as the General Assembly. They carry legal authority and influence later negotiations and litigation, but unlike judgments in contentious cases they are not binding. Individuals cannot request them.

questions.stem: The International Criminal Court (ICC) was set up by the:
options: UN Charter of 1945, as a principal organ of the UN
Geneva Conventions of 1949, after the Second World War
Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948
Rome Statute of 1998, which came into force in 2002
questions.explanation: The ICC is a permanent court created by the Rome Statute, adopted in 1998, which came into force on 1 July 2002. It is independent of the UN, unlike the ICJ, which was set up by the UN Charter.

questions.stem: The ICC has jurisdiction over which crimes?
options: Genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression
Terrorism, drug trafficking, piracy and people smuggling
Genocide, torture, slavery and breaches of the Refugee Convention
Crimes against humanity, corruption, money laundering and fraud
questions.explanation: Article 5 of the Rome Statute limits the court to the four most serious crimes of international concern: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. Terrorism and drug trafficking are dealt with by national courts.

questions.stem: When Australia ratified the Rome Statute in 2002, the Commonwealth also inserted offences of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes into the Criminal Code (Cth). What was the main reason?
options: To give state courts the power to hear appeals from the ICC
To allow Australia to prosecute these crimes itself, so the ICC need not act
To transfer all Australian criminal cases to the ICC for trial in The Hague
To stop Australian citizens being tried for these crimes by any court
questions.explanation: The ICC is complementary to national courts: it acts only when a state is unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute. By creating the offences in Division 268 of the Criminal Code, Australia ensured it could deal with such crimes in its own courts first.

questions.stem: After the Afghanistan Inquiry report (2020) found credible information of unlawful killings by some Australian soldiers, the government set up the Office of the Special Investigator. How does this relate to the ICC?
options: The ICC cannot act because Australia withdrew from the Rome Statute after the report
The ICJ, rather than the ICC, would try the soldiers if Australia did not act
Under complementarity, a genuine national investigation means the ICC need not act
The ICC must take over the case, because war crimes can be tried only in The Hague
questions.explanation: Under complementarity, a case is inadmissible at the ICC if a state with jurisdiction is genuinely investigating or prosecuting it. Australia remains a party to the Rome Statute. The ICJ does not try individuals.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant practical weakness of the ICC?
options: It can try only people who are nationals of the five permanent Security Council members
It has no power to imprison anyone it convicts of an international crime
It can hear cases only when the accused agrees to its jurisdiction
It has no police force, so it depends on states to arrest and surrender suspects
questions.explanation: The ICC relies on states to carry out its arrest warrants and surrender suspects, so people sheltered by their own or friendly governments may never be tried. Several major powers are not parties. The court can impose imprisonment on those it convicts.

questions.stem: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly rather than ratified by states. What is the main legal implication for Australia?
options: It binds only the states that signed it in 1948, so Australia is not affected
It has no relevance, because Australia has its own national bill of rights
It is not binding as a treaty, but it guides later treaties and obligations
It binds Australia directly, so courts must invalidate laws inconsistent with it
questions.explanation: The UDHR is a declaration of the General Assembly, not a treaty, so it was never signed or ratified. Its principles shaped the binding covenants and many of its rights are widely seen as reflecting customary international law. Australia has no national bill of rights.

questions.stem: As a party to the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, Australia's main obligation is to:
options: apply the Convention's protections without time or geographic limits
accept every person who applies for asylum as a permanent citizen within a year
resettle any refugee that UNHCR refers to it from any country in the world
give refugees the right to vote in federal elections once they arrive
questions.explanation: By joining the Protocol, Australia agreed to apply the Convention's definition and protections, including non-refoulement, to refugees from any place and time. The Convention does not oblige states to grant citizenship or resettle every person UNHCR refers.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980 is to:
options: secure the prompt return of a child wrongfully taken to or kept in another country
decide which parent should have custody of a child after an overseas divorce
punish parents who take their children overseas without a court's permission
set the age at which a child can choose to live in another country
questions.explanation: The Convention aims to return a wrongfully removed or retained child promptly to the country of their habitual residence, so that the courts there can decide parenting arrangements. It does not decide custody itself and it is civil, not criminal.

questions.stem: A father takes his eight-year-old daughter from Brisbane to another country without the mother's consent. Both countries are parties to the Hague Abduction Convention. Which Australian body would help the mother seek the child's return?
options: The Australian Human Rights Commission
The Commonwealth Central Authority in the Attorney-General's Department
The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
questions.explanation: Each party appoints a Central Authority; Australia's is in the Commonwealth Attorney-General's Department, working with state central authorities. It applies to the other country's central authority, and that country's courts decide whether to order the return.

questions.stem: A mother takes her child from Queensland to a country that is not a party to the Hague Abduction Convention. What is the main implication for the father?
options: The Convention still applies, because Australia ratified it on behalf of all countries
The ICJ will order the child's return once the father lodges a complaint with it
The Convention requires the other country to extradite the mother to Australia
The Convention's return process is unavailable, so that country's law applies
questions.explanation: Treaties bind only the states that are parties, so the Convention's system works only between countries that have both joined it. Otherwise the parent must use the other country's courts or diplomacy. Individuals cannot bring cases to the ICJ.

questions.stem: In a Hague Abduction Convention case, a court may refuse to return a child if:
options: the parent who took the child earns more and can give the child a better education
the child has been in the new country for at least one week and has started school
the parent who took the child is a citizen of the country to which the child was taken
return would expose the child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm
questions.explanation: Article 13(b) allows refusal where return would expose the child to a grave risk of harm or an intolerable situation. Other exceptions include consent or acquiescence and, where proceedings start more than a year after removal, the child being settled. Wealth and nationality are not grounds.

questions.stem: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples was adopted in 2007. Australia voted against it at the time but formally endorsed it in 2009. What is its legal effect in Australia?
options: It is binding because Australia ratified it at a referendum in 2009
It has no effect, because declarations can only be endorsed by the Security Council
It is not a binding treaty, so it guides policy but is not enforceable in courts
It became part of Australian law in 2009 and overrides inconsistent state laws
questions.explanation: A declaration of the General Assembly is not a treaty and creates no binding obligations. Endorsement is a political commitment that can guide law reform and policy, but the declaration is not enforceable unless parliament legislates.

questions.stem: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 mainly protect:
options: people not or no longer fighting, such as the wounded, prisoners and civilians
the territorial integrity of states from invasion by their neighbours
refugees who have fled persecution and crossed an international border
states' rights to choose which weapons they use in an armed conflict
questions.explanation: The Geneva Conventions protect wounded and sick soldiers on land and at sea, prisoners of war and civilians in armed conflict. Refugees are protected by the Refugee Convention, and limits on weapons and methods of warfare come mainly from the Hague Conventions.

questions.stem: International humanitarian law is sometimes divided into 'Hague law' and 'Geneva law'. Which statement best describes the difference?
options: Hague law limits the means and methods of warfare; Geneva law protects victims of war
Hague law applies only in peacetime; Geneva law applies only during armed conflict
Hague law binds individuals; Geneva law binds only states and their armies
Hague law protects refugees; Geneva law sets out the rights of children
questions.explanation: The Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 regulate the conduct of hostilities, including lawful weapons and tactics, while the 1949 Geneva Conventions protect people who are not or no longer fighting. Both apply during armed conflict.

questions.stem: Australia is a party to the Geneva Conventions. Which domestic step best gives effect to this?
options: Allowing the ICJ to hear appeals from Australian military courts
Making grave breaches of the Conventions offences under Commonwealth law
Giving the Red Cross power to try soldiers accused of breaches
Requiring every soldier to swear an oath to the UN Secretary-General
questions.explanation: Australia implemented the Conventions through the Geneva Conventions Act 1957 (Cth), and war crimes are now offences in the Criminal Code (Cth). This lets Australian courts prosecute breaches. The ICRC promotes humanitarian law but does not try anyone.

questions.stem: In Queensland a child can be held criminally responsible from age 10. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child recommends a minimum age of at least 14. Which statement best evaluates Queensland's position?
options: It is invalid, because the Committee's recommendation overrides the Criminal Code
It meets international standards, because the Convention sets the minimum age at 10
It is invalid, because section 109 makes the Convention prevail over state law
It is lawful in Queensland but criticised as below international standards
questions.explanation: Section 29 of the Criminal Code (Qld) sets the age of criminal responsibility at 10. The Committee's recommendation is not binding, and an unincorporated treaty cannot override state law through section 109, which applies only to Commonwealth legislation. The gap attracts sustained criticism from UN bodies and advocates.

questions.stem: Article 37 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child says the detention of a child should be:
options: in an adult prison, so that the child can be properly supervised
permitted only with the written consent of the child's parents
a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time
used whenever a child is charged with an offence carrying a prison term
questions.explanation: Article 37(b) requires that arrest, detention or imprisonment of a child be used only as a last resort and for the shortest appropriate time, and that children be separated from adults. Holding children in police watch houses has been criticised against this standard.

questions.stem: A Commonwealth law requires certain social media platforms to take reasonable steps to stop children under 16 holding accounts. Which pair of rights in the Convention on the Rights of the Child is most clearly in tension?
options: The child's right to a nationality and the child's right to rest and leisure
The child's right to vote and the child's protection from economic exploitation
Protection from harm and freedom of expression and access to information
The child's right to an education and the child's right to a fair trial
questions.explanation: Supporters argue the law protects children's health and safety online, while critics argue it limits their rights to expression, information and participation. Evaluating such laws involves weighing competing rights. Children have no right to vote under the Convention.

questions.stem: The Termination of Pregnancy Act 2018 (Qld) allows a medical practitioner to perform a termination on a person who is more than 22 weeks pregnant if the practitioner:
options: has obtained the approval of a judge of the Supreme Court of Queensland
has the written consent of the pregnant person's spouse or partner
is satisfied that the pregnancy resulted from a criminal offence
thinks it should be performed and another practitioner consulted agrees
questions.explanation: Under section 6, after 22 weeks the practitioner must consider that, in all the circumstances, the termination should be performed, and must consult another practitioner who agrees. Up to 22 weeks a termination is available on request under section 5. No court approval or partner consent is required.

questions.stem: The Termination of Pregnancy Act 2018 (Qld) creates safe access zones, generally 150 metres around termination services. Which competing rights must be balanced?
options: Doctors' right to strike against patients' right to choose their own doctor
Police powers of arrest against the right of protesters to a jury trial
Patients' right to vote against protesters' freedom of religion
Patients' privacy and safe access to care against protesters' expression
questions.explanation: Safe access zones protect the privacy, dignity and safety of people using health services, but limit the expression and assembly of protesters nearby. The High Court upheld similar zones in other states against the implied freedom of political communication in Clubb v Edwards (2019).

questions.stem: The Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of People with Disability (2019-2023) made many recommendations. How does it best relate to Australia's international obligations?
options: It was required by the CRPD, which orders a royal commission in every state party
It replaced the CRPD Committee as the body that reviews Australia's reports
It had power to strike down laws inconsistent with the Disability Discrimination Act
It examined how well Australia meets its CRPD obligations and recommended changes
questions.explanation: The royal commission investigated failures to protect people with disability and drew on the rights in the CRPD in its recommendations. Royal commissions inquire and recommend; they cannot invalidate laws, and the CRPD Committee continues to review Australia's reports.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the effectiveness of international law in protecting human rights in Australia?
options: International law has no effect in Australia, because treaties cannot influence domestic law
International courts can strike down any Australian law that breaches a ratified treaty
Monitoring creates pressure, but implementation is left to parliament
International bodies can enforce their findings directly, so Australia's laws always comply
questions.explanation: Reporting, reviews and complaints have influenced Australian reforms, as in the response to Toonen. But treaties are not enforceable until parliament legislates, and international bodies cannot compel compliance, so outcomes depend on political will.
